Battle of Iwo Jima. Fought from February to March nineteen forty-five, the Battle of Iwo Jima saw American forces assault one of the most heavily fortified Japanese island positions in the Pacific. The thirty-five-day campaign to capture the small volcanic island cost the U.S. Marines nearly seven thousand lives and resulted in an iconic photograph of flag-raising atop Mount Suribachi that became an enduring symbol of American sacrifice.

The island is located twelve hundred kilometers south of Tokyo and was strategic as a base for fighter escort for B-29 bombers raiding Japan. The Japanese garrison of approximately twenty-one thousand soldiers was commanded by General Tomoshiro Kamatube and dug into fortified cave positions and tunnels. The American assault force numbered nearly seventy thousand Marines under General Holland Smith, with three Marine divisions landing on black sand beaches.

On February twenty-third, Marines captured Mount Suribachi, and photographer Joe Rosenthal captured the iconic image of Marines raising the American flag atop it, a photograph that won the Pulitzer Prize. The fighting that followed was the fiercest in the Pacific. U.S. casualties reached sixty-eight hundred twenty-one killed, with over nineteen thousand wounded, while Japanese losses exceeded eighteen thousand, with very few surrendering. The island was secured by March twenty-sixth, nineteen forty-five, providing a forward base for fighter-escort operations and an emergency airfield for damaged B-29s. This tactical victory demonstrated the immense cost of assaulting heavily defended Japanese territories, foreshadowing the even greater losses that would come at Okinawa.
